newsitem.title: UK: U.N. invites Morocco, Polisario to Lisbon talks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. invites Morocco, Polisario to Lisbon talks.

text.p: U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan on Thursday invited Morocco and the Polisario Front movement struggling for independence in Western Sahara to hold face-to-face talks in Lisbon on June 23.

Former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker, Annan's envoy to the region, said after two days of meetings with all those involved that there was a growing realisation the Lisbon talks might be the last real chance of solving the area's problems.
"I have come to the conclusion that in the absence of direct talks between the parties involved, I do not think it (a U.N. plan to settle the conflict) can be concluded," Baker told reporters.

He said Morocco and the Polisario had indicated they were prepared to make concessions to try to end the dispute, which dates back to 1976 when Spain withdrew from Western Sahara and Morocco moved in.
But he added: "This doesn't mean we'll succeed. At least it means things are back on track."
A September 1991 ceasefire ended a protracted brushfire war between the two sides but around 170,000 refugees from the region still live in southern Algeria.
Algeria and Mauritania, both closely concerned with the issue, have been invited to the Lisbon talks as observers.
The United Nations has been trying for years to organise a referendum to decide whether Western Sahara should be incorporated into Morocco or become independent.
But the ballot has been repeatedly postponed because of a disagreement between the two sides over who should be eligible to vote.
"Assuming the parties accept the secretary-general's invitation, we may find a way to implement the settlement," said Baker, stressing that there was still much to be achieved.

"There is some indication that the parties see this as the last best chance to get it implemented," he added, saying that neither side was interested in the idea of Western Sahara being granted some form of limited autonomy.
The Polisario wants the referendum to be limited to the 75,000 people registered as living in Western Sahara in 1974 while Morocco wants the 120,000 people who have since moved there to be included.

Baker said Morocco was now prepared to put off a decision on whether about 60,000 of the new settlers should take part while the Polisario had agreed to stop boycotting attempts to identify who was eligible to vote.

Baker has to advise Annan whether the U.N. plan can still be implemented in its present form, whether adjustments acceptable to the two sides might be possible or whether other ways of resolving the conflict could be found.
The Security Council last month renewed until September 30 the mandate of a 230-member U.N. observer force called the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara.
